plain_english: Let me explain this, since we both agree these things are desirable. Here's why I count them among good things, and how I'd act differently from you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Put me where gold and silver dishes are used for everyday meals. I won't think more of myself because of these things. Even though they're in my house, they're not part of who I am. Now take me away to the wooden bridge and drop me there among the beggars. I won't despise myself because I'm sitting among people who hold out their hands for money. What does it matter if I lack a piece of bread when I don't lack the power to die? So what's my point? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.
original_excerpt: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.

plain_english: Put me in a mansion filled with luxury. I won't think I'm any happier just because my clothes are soft or my guests sit on purple cushions. Now change the scene completely. I won't be more miserable if my tired head rests on a pile of hay, or if I sleep on a torn circus cushion with stuffing poking out through holes in the worn fabric. So what's my point? I do prefer to appear in public wearing fine wool and official robes rather than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like my daily business to go exactly as I want it to, with one success following another. But I won't let this make me proud. Now flip all this good fortune upside down. Let my mind be torn apart by losses, grief, and different kinds of attacks. Let no hour pass without some argument. Even surrounded by the greatest miseries, I still won't call myself the most wretched person alive. I won't curse any particular day, because I've made sure I have no unlucky days.
original_excerpt: Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple. Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days.

plain_english: So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than struggle to overcome my sorrows. The great Socrates would tell you the same thing. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations. Let Bacchus's luxurious chariot carry me in triumph from the sunrise all the way to Thebes. Let the Persian kings receive their laws from me. Even then, I'll still know I'm just a man, right when everyone around me is calling me a god. Now flip this completely — let me fall headfirst into disaster. Put me on a foreign chariot to decorate some cruel conqueror's triumph. I'll follow behind his chariot with no more shame than I showed when I rode in my own. So what? Even with all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the captive."
original_excerpt: What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows. The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive."

plain_english: I despise everything Fortune controls, but honestly, if I had to choose, I'd pick the good parts. I can turn whatever happens to me into something good, but I'd rather have things that are comfortable and pleasant and don't annoy me. Don't think that virtue comes without effort — but some virtues need to be pushed forward, while others need to be held back. Just like we have to hold our body back on a steep downhill path and push it up a steep climb, some virtues take us downhill and others uphill.
original_excerpt: I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb. As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill.

plain_english: Can we doubt that patience, courage, and steadiness — all the virtues that face strong opposition and crush Fortune under their feet — are climbing a steep mountain? They struggle and fight their way up. But isn't it just as clear that generosity, moderation, and gentleness roll easily downhill? With those easy virtues, we must hold back our spirit so it doesn't run away with us. With the hard virtues, we must push and drive ourselves forward. So we should use these tough, fighting virtues when we're poor. And when we're rich, we should use those other careful virtues that move lightly and just carry their own weight.
original_excerpt: Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight.

plain_english: Since there's a difference between these types of challenges, I'd rather deal with the ones I can practice in relative peace than those you can only test through blood and sweat. "That's why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. But you don't really understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words — you don't try to figure out what they actually mean."
original_excerpt: This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
